title: What makes Z-Wave special?
notes: Z-Wave defines the radio, network behavior, and device commands. Standardized commands let compatible products from different manufacturers understand the same request. Battery devices can save energy through short transmissions and sleep; many actuators are mains-powered. The diagram shows one successful delivery — ACKs, retries and frame fields belong on later slides.
html:
What makes Z-Wave special?

Sub-GHz

Regional frequency bands below 1 GHz.

Low throughput

Small commands and reports.

Low power

Battery-friendly operation.

Standardized

Device behavior across manufacturers — radio, network and meaning.

title: Inside a Z-Wave frame
notes: The same three command bytes stay visible at every stage. The MAC adds delivery information and a checksum; the PHY adds synchronization. This is an unencrypted, unrouted example for an on/off lamp that supports Basic control — FF means on for this device, and all byte values are hexadecimal. The checksum starts at FF and XORs the twelve preceding MAC bytes to produce 60: it detects corruption, but sender authentication needs security at another layer. The solid rows are the minimum-preamble 40 kbit/s example; at 100 kbit/s the two-channel preamble is at least 40 bytes and the FCS becomes a two-byte CRC.
html:
Inside a Z-Wave frame

MAC frame

Addresses — network 12 34 56 78, from node 1 to node 7.

Control 41 03 — singlecast, ACK requested, sequence number 3.

Length 0D — 13 bytes, including the FCS.

FCS / CRC* 60 — one-byte XOR over the preceding MAC bytes; a two-byte CRC-16 at 100 kbit/s.

PHY frame

Preamble 55 — 01010101 repeated for receiver synchronization.

SOF F0 — 11110000 marks the start of the MAC frame.

EOF* — required at 9.6 kbit/s. Eight Manchester code violations end the transmission.

title: Source routing
notes: Only the next repeater named by the route position forwards this frame. It receives and validates the frame, advances the hop position, and recalculates the FCS before transmitting a fresh radio frame. The ordered list stays in the frame throughout delivery. Repeaters follow the source's selected path. The MAC header is 9 bytes. The routing header adds 4 bytes. Basic Set occupies 3 bytes and FCS occupies 1 byte. The length field is therefore 11 hex, or 17 bytes. This is an unencrypted, two-channel example with always-listening nodes and no routing extensions. It stops at destination reception. Acknowledgment behavior belongs on the following slide.
html:
Hopping through the mesh 🐇

  • Source routing: The sender puts an ordered repeater list in the frame.
  • Forwarding: Each repeater advances the hop position, recomputes the checksum, and transmits.
  • Unchanged: The original source, destination, repeater list, and command.

title: Acknowledgments
notes: The repeated DATA frame itself provides the implicit acknowledgment. Returning Routed ACKs use the same overhearing mechanism between repeaters. Node 7's Routed ACK confirms the last DATA hop. This normal sequence has no preceding ordinary ACK from node 7 to node 3. Node 1 receives end-to-end delivery confirmation when the Routed ACK reaches it. Its final ordinary ACK confirms the last returning hop to node 2. This is the normal silent-ACK exchange with always-listening nodes. Beaming and explicitly requested additional ACKs are outside this example.
html:
Acknowledgments: direct and routed

  • Implicit ACK: Hearing the next node forward confirms that hop.
  • Routed ACK: Node 7 returns delivery confirmation along the reverse route.
  • Final ACK: Node 1 confirms receipt of node 2’s returning frame.

title: Missing ACKs: direct
notes: Ask the title question, pause, then repeat it when revealing a retry. Both direct cases look the same to the sender: it has no confirmation, and the destination may already have received DATA. G.9959 permits two retries after the initial transmission, with a 10-40 ms random backoff; ACK waiting is separate. Both examples succeed on their first retry. Exhausted direct retries report NO_ACK upward as a local status.
html:
Missing ACKs · direct

title: Local retries and Routed Error
notes: In routed traffic every forwarding transmitter can face the same uncertainty; this diagram shows only the last hop failing. Returning Routed ACKs and Routed Errors can also be lost and retried locally. A Routed Error means forwarding could not be confirmed — from DATA loss or from loss of the next node's confirmation. If neither a Routed ACK nor a Routed Error reaches the source, its end-to-end timer expires. Node 1's final ACK confirms only that the error arrived; the application command was not delivered. Attempt counts and further rate or route recovery depend on the stack and transmit options. Explorer discovery is the next slide.
html:
Missing ACKs · routed

Would you like to hear a Z-Wave joke?

A repeater reports a forwarding failure back to the source, which can then try another route.

title: Retry, reroute, explore
notes: First, retry the transmission — an eligible direct send can try 100, 100, then 40 kbit/s. If that still fails, the controller can try another cached path or calculate alternatives. Eventually an enabled explorer fallback can discover a path through nearby repeaters, carrying the command as it goes. The destination returns a Search Result along the first successful path, giving the sender a route it can reuse. The left column is a simplified, conditional controller policy: missing routes and disabled options skip stages, and each selected path has its own attempt sequence. G.9959 itself only defines the initial send plus up to two retries with 10-40 ms random backoff; the ladder is implementation policy, not a MAC rule.
html: Retry, reroute, explore

title: The same command at three speeds
notes: Manchester uses two radio symbols per data bit. NRZ uses one. GFSK smooths the frequency transitions. “The command is identical at every speed. At 9.6 kbit/s, this one transmission takes about 24 milliseconds. At 40 it takes 5.6. At 100 it takes 4.7. The longer 100 kbit/s preamble limits the gain for such a small command. The slowest rate still occupies the radio for over four times as long as 40 kbit/s. Repeaters and retries multiply that airtime.” The three DATA transmissions through two repeaters sum to 72.5 ms, 16.8 ms, or 14.16 ms respectively. ACKs and waiting add further overhead. The 100 kbit/s format also permits larger MAC frames: 170 bytes versus 64 bytes. Other regional channel configurations have different preamble and header sizes.
html: The same command at three speeds

title: One radio, hopping through channels 🦘
notes: “The receiver samples several profiles. A preamble gives it time to visit the matching profile and synchronize. It can join partway through the preamble. Once it finds the start of the frame, it stays to receive the data. When the radio is free again, scanning resumes. An LR frame can pass completely during a long 9.6 reception. The LR sender may see a clear channel and still get no ACK.” Accuracy: the four-profile example is a combined classic/LR controller — three classic receive modes and one selected LR channel, A or B. Profiles include frequency, modulation, coding and timing settings. Preamble/timing detection can extend the channel visit; SOF synchronization starts frame reception; header rejection, reception errors or acquisition timeouts can release the receiver earlier. The MAC length field determines the expected frame length, and FCS validation is part of accepting the frame. The small finish interval leaves room for required response handling; ACK transmission and exact radio state transitions are omitted, so the graphic does not imply immediate hopping before a required ACK. Hop dwell times and frame-part widths are schematic.
html:
One radio, hopping through channels 🦘

  • Scan: One receiver visits several radio profiles.
  • Acquire: A matching preamble gives it time to synchronize.
  • Receive: After SOF detection, it stays for the frame.

title: Scotty, beam me up
notes: “A frequently-listening device checks its radio briefly. A beam repeats addressed wake-up frames long enough to overlap one of those checks. Classic two-channel Z-Wave uses short or long continuous trains. Fragmented beams insert gaps. A beam acknowledgment can stop that train early, then DATA follows. This uses airtime before the application command is sent.” Ordinary sleeping sensors use their own wake-up schedule; beaming requires a device designed for frequently-listening operation. In a routed exchange, the final repeater can perform the beaming. Timing: short continuous 275 ms recommended (300 ms max), long 1100 ms (1160 ms max), fragments 110–115 ms with 190–200 ms start spacing and a 3000 ms full train. The 275/1100 ms recommendations come from G.9959; the 250/1000 ms labels are listening intervals, and firmware timing can differ. The fragmented pattern also exists in classic three-channel regions, so it is not exclusive to LR; LR requires a receiver accepting a singlecast beam to interrupt the train with an ACK, and the classic specification permits it. Every beam frame carries its own preamble and SOF, so a device waking late can catch a later frame. The beam tag distinguishes the frame from a normal Home-ID-led MAC frame; the hash filters wake-up requests and does not authenticate the sender. Broadcast-beam acknowledgment rules and LR chip encoding are out of scope.
html: Scotty, beam me awake
